content: Kawasaki disease, also referred to as lymph node syndrome, mucocutaneous node disease, infantile polyarteritis, or Kawasaki syndrome, is a self-limited vasculitis that affects multiple organ systems, including the skin, mucous membranes, lymph nodes, blood vessel walls, and the heart. It is not considered contagious. The disease was first described in 1967 by Dr. Tomisaku Kawasaki in Japan. It primarily affects young children, with 80% of cases occurring in those under 5 years of age. In the United States, additional risk factors include being of Asian descent and male sex. Kawasaki disease can lead to inflammation of the coronary arteries (vasculitis), which may result in coronary artery aneurysms. Common symptoms include high-grade fever, red eyes, bright red and cracked lips, red mucous membranes in the mouth, a strawberry tongue (characterized by a white coating or prominent red bumps on the tongue), red palms and soles, swollen hands and feet, and a rash. Treatment typically involves intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and aspirin. Dr. Tomisaku Kawasaki first encountered the disease in 1961 in Japan and published his findings in 1967. He later established the Japan Kawasaki Disease Research Center in 1990. Patients who do not meet the full diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki disease but exhibit fever and coronary artery abnormalities are classified as having atypical or incomplete Kawasaki disease. In such cases, evidence of coronary abnormalities or coronary artery aneurysms (CAAs) must be demonstrated via echocardiography. The exact cause of Kawasaki disease remains unknown, but it is believed to result from environmental, viral, or genetic factors. The disease involves systemic inflammation of medium-sized arteries and multiple organs, which can lead to associated conditions such as hepatitis, interstitial pneumonitis, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, gallbladder hydrops, aseptic meningitis, irritability, myocarditis, pericarditis, valvulitis, pyuria, pancreatitis, and lymphadenopathy. Pathological findings may include large or giant coronary artery aneurysms, thrombosed aneurysms, luminal narrowing, stenosis, and chronic inflammation. Microscopic analysis of autopsied cases often reveals intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in ciliated bronchial epithelial cells. The precise etiology of Kawasaki disease has not been identified. Current theories focus on immunological causes, and ongoing research aims to identify a definitive toxin or antigenic substance, possibly a superantigen, as the trigger. Infectious agents potentially linked to Kawasaki disease include parvovirus B19, adenovirus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and others. Kawasaki disease must be differentiated from other conditions that cause rash-like symptoms, such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis, measles, scarlet fever, toxic shock syndrome, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, among others. Epidemiologically, Kawasaki disease occurs worldwide, with the highest incidence in Japan. It predominantly affects boys and younger children, with a possible seasonal pattern in winter and spring. In the United States, the incidence ranges from 9 to 19 cases per 100,000 children under 5 years old. In 2000, approximately 4,248 hospitalizations for Kawasaki disease were reported in the U.S., with 77% involving children under 5 years of age. Risk factors for Kawasaki disease include a combination of environmental, genetic, and viral influences. Routine screening for Kawasaki disease is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. If left untreated, symptoms of Kawasaki disease may resolve, but coronary artery aneurysms will persist, increasing the risk of myocardial infarction, disability, or death. Timely treatment can significantly reduce these risks and shorten the disease course. Long-term complications may include coronary artery disease and premature atherosclerosis. Common complications include vasculitis and coronary artery aneurysms. The prognosis is generally excellent, with a mortality rate of approximately 2%. Kawasaki disease is diagnosed clinically, as there are no specific laboratory tests for confirmation. Diagnosis can be challenging, especially early in the disease course, and children are often not diagnosed until they have seen a physician multiple times. The diagnostic criteria include five days of fever plus four of the following: mucositis (erythema of the palatine mucosa), fissured erythematous lips, strawberry tongue, rash (polymorphous, often urticarial, and erythematous, primarily on the extremities but may spread to the trunk), extremity changes (edema of hands and feet, erythema of palms and soles, desquamation of fingertips), and cervical lymphadenopathy of at least 15 millimeters. Kawasaki disease often begins with a high, persistent fever that does not respond well to standard doses of acetaminophen or ibuprofen. The fever may last up to two weeks and is typically accompanied by irritability. Affected children may develop red eyes, mucous membranes, and lips, a strawberry tongue, iritis, keratic precipitates (detectable by an ophthalmologist), and swollen lymph nodes. Skin rashes appear early, and peeling of the skin on the hands, feet, and genital area may occur later. Symptoms may wax and wane during the illness. Physical examination findings in Kawasaki disease include erythematous rash, irritability, and desquamation of the skin and mucous membranes. Laboratory investigations may reveal elevated C-reactive protein, hyponatremia, and sterile pyuria. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) in Kawasaki disease may show evidence of ventricular dysfunction or arrhythmias due to myocarditis. Acute disease may also present with prolonged PR intervals, nonspecific ST changes, T-wave changes, and increased Q/R ratios, consistent with myocarditis. Chest X-rays may reveal nonspecific findings such as peribronchial cuffing, reticulogranular patterns, pleural effusion, atelectasis, and air trapping. In rare cases, coronary artery calcifications may be visualized years after the initial episode, particularly in older patients. Echocardiography is useful in diagnosing Kawasaki disease, with findings such as coronary artery dilations, stenoses, or aneurysms. Ultrasound may reveal gallbladder hydrops. CT angiography can aid in diagnosis by identifying small coronary artery dilations, aneurysms, or stenoses. Angiography is the most sensitive and specific method for assessing vessel involvement. MRI findings are not directly associated with Kawasaki disease, but magnetic resonance angiography can accurately define coronary artery aneurysms in affected patients. Other diagnostic studies, including urinalysis, lumbar puncture, biomarkers, and angiography, may support the diagnosis. Findings may include leukocytosis, white blood cells in the urine, and coronary artery aneurysms. Treatment involves intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and aspirin, which should be initiated promptly to prevent coronary artery damage. Aspirin is an exception in children with Kawasaki disease, as it is otherwise avoided due to its association with Reye's syndrome. Hospitalization is recommended for affected children. In cases of coronary artery compromise, mechanical revascularization may be attempted. Primary prevention of Kawasaki disease is not applicable, but complications can be mitigated through medical prophylaxis.
